paragraph.text: B12. "Foie gras is a traditional delicacy, and ducks naturally eat a lot"

foie gras is the diseased liver of ducks and geese force-fed through a tube pushed down the throat, two or three times a day, in the last weeks of their lives, until the organ grows several times its size. It's true that these birds store fat before migrating, but none of them eats like this of its own accord. Forcing food into someone who doesn't need it and making an animal ill on purpose, for a luxury dish, is a serious harm, and several countries have banned the practice.
"Foie gras is a French culinary tradition. And ducks naturally eat a lot; they fatten up on their own before migrating."
Wild ducks and geese store fat in their livers before migrating.
Foie gras production only enhances this natural capacity.
Foie gras is an old gastronomic tradition.
So producing and eating foie gras is acceptable.
P1 is true. P2 fails: production doesn't let the bird eat more, it forces food through a tube in amounts the bird wouldn't eat. P3 is true, but tradition doesn't justify harm (D1).
"Ducks fatten up on their own before migrating."
"It's a delicacy, eaten on special occasions."
"Now they want to ban foie gras too?"
"Geese have a natural physiological capacity to store fat in the liver."

To make foie gras, people put a tube down a duck's throat and push in lots of food, several times a day, until its liver becomes huge and sick. The duck doesn't choose to eat that much. It would be like someone stuffing food into you when you're already full.

Do you know how it's made? Foie gras is the diseased liver of force-fed ducks and geese: a tube is pushed down the throat, two or three times a day, in the last weeks of life, until the liver grows several times its size. These birds store fat before migrating, but none eats like this of its own accord. Pushing food into someone who doesn't need it, until the liver is made ill on purpose, is a serious harm, not a detail of the recipe. Being a tradition changes nothing for the duck. Several countries have banned it.
"If the duck fattened up on its own, why would a tube down its throat be needed?"
"The duck fattens up on its own"
Food is pushed through a tube, in amounts far above the natural
The liver grows several times its size and becomes diseased (steatosis)
The current industrial technique, with individual cages, is recent

text.bold: 1. The bird doesn't eat; it's force-fed.

paragraph.text: In production, ducks and geese are fed through a tube two or three times a day, for about two weeks in the case of ducks and a little longer for geese.

text.bold: 2. Making someone ill on purpose is serious.

paragraph.text: Force-feeding doesn't answer hunger: it pushes food into an animal that doesn't need it. According to the 1998 European scientific report, the total amount ingested is much greater than the birds would eat of their own accord, and when force-feeding stops, they greatly reduce their food intake for several days. The goal is to produce hepatic steatosis, a build-up of fat in the liver, which grows to 6 to 10 times its normal size. The report notes that no normal animal has steatosis to that degree, that liver function is impaired, and that most of the pathologists consulted considered the condition pathological; some disagree, pointing out that the steatosis is often reversible. But production itself stops in time because, if it continued, mortality would rise sharply, largely from liver failure. Even so, mortality during the force-feeding period is 2% to 4%, against around 0.2% in ducks that aren't force-fed. If someone made a person ill on purpose, it would be seen as serious violence; here, making the animal ill is the production method itself.

The EU Scientific Committee on Animal Health and Animal Welfare (SCAHAW) concluded in 1998 that force-feeding, as practiced, harms the birds' welfare. The report noted that the birds avoided the person who force-fed them, unlike what happens with ordinary hand-feeding, and that 80% of ducks were kept in individual cages.
Israel, once a major producer, banned force-feeding in 2005, and the practice is banned in several European countries, though many still import the product.
Many old practices were abandoned once the suffering they caused was recognized (D1).

The most serious version points out that some producers make fatty liver by letting birds eat freely before migration, without force-feeding.

paragraph.text: Force-feeding a dog until its liver became diseased would be cruelty.
The prestige of "traditional" makes the product seem good in every way and hides the current method

The principle being tested is: "if a bird has a natural capacity, forcing it to the extreme is acceptable".
Forcing a cow to produce milk beyond her limit
It would be acceptable if it naturally fattens
They were based on welfare evidence
It's true that foie gras has a long history and that wild ducks and geese store fat before migrating. It's also true that there are attempts to produce it without force-feeding.
But what's sold as foie gras comes almost entirely from force-feeding, which European science itself assessed as harmful to the birds. Tradition explains the recipe; it doesn't justify the method.
